questions.question: Which class does the Compose compiler infer as stable (assuming it is compiled with the Compose compiler)?
options: data class A(var count: Int)
data class B(val items: List<String>)
data class C(val name: String, val age: Int)
class D(val list: ArrayList<Int>) // plain class
questions.explanation: All properties of C are vals of stable types, so it is stable. A `var` makes A unstable because it can change without notifying Compose. List is an interface that might be mutable underneath, so B is unstable, and ArrayList is plainly mutable.

questions.question: Strong skipping mode is enabled by default for projects that use the Compose compiler from Kotlin 2.0.20 onwards.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Strong skipping became the default in Kotlin 2.0.20. It makes composables with unstable parameters skippable and memoizes lambdas with unstable captures. It can still be turned off in the composeCompiler Gradle configuration, but that is rarely needed.

questions.question: Under strong skipping, how are parameters compared to decide whether to skip?
options: Stable ones with equals(), unstable ones by instance (===)
All parameters with equals(), whatever their stability
All parameters by instance (===), whatever their stability
Unstable ones with equals(), stable ones by hashCode()
questions.explanation: Strong skipping keeps equals() for stable types and uses referential equality for unstable ones, since an unstable object's equals might change over time. So passing the same unstable instance skips, but an equal-but-new unstable instance recomposes.

questions.question: Why does the compiler treat a parameter of type List<T> as unstable?
options: List has no equals implementation the compiler can call
It may be backed by a mutable list that changes in place
Generic types are always unstable regardless of the argument
List is defined in Java, and all Java types are unstable
questions.explanation: Kotlin's List is a read-only view, not a guarantee of immutability: a MutableList can be passed as a List and changed underneath. The compiler can't prove it won't change, so it's unstable. Options are kotlinx immutable collections, a stability config entry, or a wrapper marked @Immutable.

questions.question: What does annotating a type with @Stable promise to the compiler? Select all that apply.
options: equals() for two given instances always returns the same result
The compiler verifies at build time that all properties are immutable
If a public property changes, composition is notified (e.g. it's backed by State)
All public properties are themselves of stable types
Instances of the type are safe to share between threads
questions.explanation: @Stable is a promise you make: equals is consistent, changes to public properties are observable by Compose, and public properties are stable. The compiler trusts it and does not check it, so a false annotation causes missed updates. It says nothing about thread-safety.

questions.question: A domain module without the Compose compiler defines `data class User(val id: String, val name: String)`. You want composables taking User to compare it with equals() rather than by instance. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Make User a value class so the compiler can inline it everywhere
Override hashCode() in User so equality is cached
Annotate User with @Serializable so its fields are known
List User in the Compose stability configuration file
questions.explanation: Classes from modules not built with the Compose compiler are treated as unstable because their stability isn't known. The stability configuration file (stabilityConfigurationFiles in composeCompiler) lets the UI module declare them stable without touching the domain module. Serialization and hashCode don't affect stability.

questions.question: Under strong skipping, a composable with an unstable parameter still recomposes every time its parent recomposes, even if exactly the same instance is passed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That was the behaviour before strong skipping. Now every restartable composable is skippable, and unstable parameters are compared with ===, so the same instance means it skips. Only a new instance (even an equal one) causes it to recompose.

questions.question: With strong skipping on, the ViewModel emits `state.copy(title = "New")`. What happens when Screen recomposes?
options: Both Header and ItemList recompose, since UiState is a new instance
Header recomposes; ItemList skips because the same list instance is passed
Neither recomposes, since UiState is a data class with equals
ItemList recomposes because List is unstable and always compares as changed
questions.explanation: copy() shares unchanged property references, so `state.items` is the same list instance and the === check lets ItemList skip. The title String changed, so Header reruns. Unstable doesn't mean 'always changed' under strong skipping; it means 'compared by instance'.

questions.question: With strong skipping on, which of these still cause extra recompositions? Select all that apply.
options: Passing `items.filter { it.visible }`, computed in the composable body, to a child
Passing a stable data class that is re-created with equal values
Reading a fast-changing state such as scroll offset in a top-level composable body
Passing a lambda that captures only the same ViewModel instance
questions.explanation: filter returns a new List every time and List is unstable, so the child's === check fails on every recomposition; remember the result keyed on items instead. Reading fast-changing state high up re-runs that whole scope. Equal stable objects pass the equals check, and lambdas with the same captures are memoized.

questions.question: How can you see which of your composables are skippable and which classes the compiler considers stable?
options: Enable Compose compiler reports and metrics in Gradle
Run Lint with the --stability flag on the app module
Open the Layout Inspector and look at each node's recomposition counts
Read the generated R.txt file in the build directory
questions.explanation: Setting reportsDestination and metricsDestination makes the compiler write per-module files listing each composable as restartable/skippable and each class's inferred stability. Layout Inspector shows recomposition counts at runtime, which is useful too, but it doesn't explain stability.
